name: Primary
overview: Artist-led contemporary visual arts organisation and charity at 33 Seely Road in the Radford neighbourhood of Nottingham, about 15 minutes' walk from the city centre (Primary site).
It is housed in a Grade II listed former school. In 2020 it bought the building to secure its long-term future (Primary site).

Registered as the charity and company Nottingham Studios, charity number 1132064. Companies House shows the company incorporated on 12 September 2006 with its registered office at Primary, 33 Seely Road.
funding_verdict: Primary: public and charitable: Arts Council England and the Paul Hamlyn Foundation as core funders, with trusts, a lottery fund and individual Friends

name: Site Gallery
overview: Contemporary art space specialising in moving image, new media and performance, at 1 Brown Street, Sheffield S1 2BS, in the Cultural Industries Quarter (Site Gallery, Wikipedia).

It began as an independent photography gallery in Walkley in 1978, was officially founded in 1979 with a grant from Yorkshire Arts under the name Untitled Gallery, and was renamed Site Gallery in 1996 (Wikipedia).

It moved to 1 Brown Street in 1988 under director Matthew Conduit (Wikipedia). A 2018 capital expansion was paid for by grants from Arts Council England, Sheffield City Council and a group of trusts (Site Gallery supporters page).
funding_verdict: Site Gallery: mixed: Arts Council England core funding, local council and trust grants, earned income

name: John Hansard Gallery
overview: Contemporary art gallery at 142-144 Above Bar Street, Southampton, part of the University of Southampton (John Hansard Gallery website).
Created in 1979 to unite two University galleries, the Photographic Gallery and the Fine Art Gallery. Named for John Henry Hansard (1895 to 1979), a University benefactor (gallery about page).
Directors: Leo Stable (1979 to 1980), Barry Barker (1980 to 1987), Professor Stephen Foster (1987 to 2017) and Woodrow Kernohan (2017 to the present) (gallery about page).
funding_verdict: John Hansard Gallery: part of the University of Southampton, with Arts Council England National Portfolio funding

name: Albuquerque Museum
aliases: Albuquerque Museum of Art and History
overview: City museum of art, history and culture at 2000 Mountain Road NW in Old Town, a division of the City of Albuquerque's Department of Arts and Culture (city website).
Established in 1967; it marks its 60th anniversary in 2027 (city website; Albuquerque Museum Foundation).
Holds about 10,000 works of art, 35,000 historical objects and more than 130,000 items in its photo archives, searchable in its e-Museum (city website).
funding_verdict: Albuquerque Museum: mainly public: the City of Albuquerque, with a private support foundation
wider_context: June 2020: the city removed the bronze statue of the conquistador Juan de Oñate from the La Jornada sculpture in front of the museum after a protest in which a man was shot and wounded (Albuquerque Journal, 2023).
The City Council heard the Arts Board's recommendations in December 2020 and postponed a decision; as of 2023 the statue remained in storage (Albuquerque Journal).
The museum's grounds held the statue, and the city that funds the museum controls its future.

name: Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA)
aliases: UC Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive
overview: The art museum and film archive of the University of California, Berkeley, at 2155 Center Street in downtown Berkeley, with galleries, a film theatre, a film library and art study centres (museum website).

Its origins go back to 1881 and the Bacon Art and Library Building, named for Henry Douglas Bacon, who gave his library, several paintings and half the building funds; the Powerhouse Gallery served from 1931 until the University Art Museum, designed by Mario Ciampi, opened on Bancroft Way in 1970 (museum website).

The collection holds nearly 25,000 works of art and 18,000 films and videos: Ming and Qing dynasty Chinese painting, Mughal Indian miniatures, Baroque painting, old master prints and drawings, early American painting, a core of fifty paintings by Hans Hofmann, works by Rothko, Frankenthaler, Reinhardt, Pollock, David Smith and Clyfford Still, Albert Bierstadt's Yosemite Winter Scene (1872) from Bacon's gift, West Coast avant-garde film, Soviet cinema and what it calls the largest collection of Japanese films outside of Japan (museum website).
funding_verdict: BAMPFA: a university museum, with foundation and federal grants listed by band and no amounts

name: Institute of Contemporary Art, Boston
overview: A contemporary art museum on Boston Harbor in the Seaport district, in a building by Diller Scofidio + Renfro opened in 2006, with the ICA Watershed, a free summer space in East Boston, and the ICA Seaport Studio for teens (museum website).
Incorporated in 1936 as the Boston Museum of Modern Art, a sister institution to New York's MoMA; it parted ways with MoMA and took the name Institute of Contemporary Art in 1948 (museum website).

The permanent collection was established in 2006 and covers painting, photography, prints and drawings, sculpture and time-based media; it includes the Barbara Lee Collection of Art by Women, 85 works of 20th- and 21st-century art, and Paul Chan's 1st Light (2005), a gift of Kimberly and James Pallotta (museum website).
funding_verdict: Institute of Contemporary Art, Boston: private, more than four fifths from contributions

name: Brandywine Museum of Art
overview: A museum of American art with a land conservancy, at 1 Hoffman's Mill Road, Chadds Ford, Pennsylvania (museum website).

A group of local residents bought endangered land known as Potts Meadow and founded the Brandywine Conservancy in 1967 under co-founder George A. 'Frolic' Weymouth's leadership, and the museum opened in 1971 in the renovated Hoffman's Mill, a gristmill built in 1864 (museum website, Our History).

What is there: a collection of American art with primary emphasis on the Brandywine region, especially the Wyeth family of artists; six galleries and more than 300 special exhibitions; the N.C. Wyeth House & Studio opened in 1996, Kuerner Farm in 2004 and Andrew Wyeth's Studio in 2012 (museum website). The pages read gave no object count.
funding_verdict: Brandywine Museum of Art: private, from donors and investment income, with corporate sponsorship

name: The Mint Museum
overview: A museum of international art and design in Charlotte with two sites: Mint Museum Uptown at the Levine Center for the Arts, 500 South Tryon Street, and Mint Museum Randolph at 2730 Randolph Road (museum website).

Established in 1936 in the building that had been the first United States branch mint, as North Carolina's first art museum; the museum acknowledges the unpaid and hidden labour of enslaved people of African ancestry who helped build it (museum website).

Archive: the Mint Museum Archives hold exhibition records, artist files, publications, photographs and digital documentation; the library at Mint Museum Randolph holds over 27,500 volumes on visual art, material culture and museum studies and is open by appointment (museum website).
funding_verdict: The Mint Museum: private gifts and endowment in city-owned buildings

name: Taft Museum of Art
overview: The Taft Museum of Art is at 316 Pike Street in downtown Cincinnati in the Baum-Longworth-Sinton-Taft house, the city's oldest wooden residence still in its original location, built around 1820 (museum website, about page).

Anna Sinton Taft and Charles Phelps Taft bequeathed their house and 530 works in 1927 and the museum opened in 1932; Anna inherited her father David Sinton's fortune in 1900 (museum website, about page).

What is there: more than 800 works, with Chinese porcelains, American furniture, European decorative arts including French Renaissance enamels and a medieval ivory sculpture, and European and American paintings by Gainsborough, Goya, Rembrandt and others; eight Robert S. Duncanson landscape murals on the entry hall walls, which became National Historic Landmarks with the house in 1976 (museum website, about page).
funding_verdict: Taft Museum of Art: mainly donations and endowment income

name: Meadows Museum
aliases: Meadows Museum at Southern Methodist University
overview: A museum of Spanish art in a two-storey Georgian-style red brick building of about 66,000 square feet at 5900 Bishop Blvd. on the SMU campus in Dallas, designed by Hammond Beeby Rupert Ainge of Chicago and opened in March 2001 (museum website).

In 1962 Algur H. Meadows, through The Meadows Foundation, gave SMU funds to build and endow a museum for his Spanish collection; it opened on 3 April 1965 in the Owen Arts Center. King Juan Carlos and Queen Sofia dedicated the 2001 building on 25 March 2001 (museum website).

What is there: a collection of Spanish art built largely by Meadows's purchases in the 1960s and 1970s and nearly doubled since, with works by Velazquez (Portrait of King Philip IV, Portrait of Queen Mariana), Goya (Yard with Madmen), El Greco, Ribera, Picasso and Dali (L'homme poisson, 1930), and outdoor works by Jaume Plensa and Santiago Calatrava. The page gave no object count (museum website).
funding_verdict: Meadows Museum: a university museum funded mainly by the founder's family foundation, built on oil wealth

name: Perot Museum of Nature and Science
overview: Perot Museum of Nature and Science, 2201 N. Field Street, Dallas, five levels of hands-on exhibits (museum website).

The Dallas Museum of Natural History (1936), The Science Place (1946) and the Dallas Children's Museum (1995) merged in 2006; in May 2008 the five children of Ross and Margot Perot gave $50 million and the museum took the Perot name.
What is there: a collections-based natural history focus; the page gives no collection count and describes no archive (museum website).
funding_verdict: Perot Museum of Nature and Science: private gifts from the Perot family and Texas donors, plus ticket income

name: James A. Michener Art Museum
overview: An art museum at 138 South Pine Street, Doylestown, Pennsylvania, in a former 19th century prison with a sculpture garden in the first courtyard (WHYY).
It opened in 1988 and took more than 20 years to transform the prison into a museum; Bruce Katsiff led it as first director (WHYY).
What is there: a large group of Pennsylvania Impressionist paintings, shown with the museum's exhibitions of Bucks County painters and writers, and the book The Genius Belt about that legacy (WHYY).
funding_verdict: James A. Michener Art Museum: private, from donors and investment income; no named funders in the pages read

name: Flint Institute of Arts
aliases: Flint Institute of Arts Museum + Art School
overview: The Flint Institute of Arts Museum + Art School is at 1120 East Kearsley Street, Flint, Michigan, on the Flint Cultural Center campus, and calls itself the second largest art museum in Michigan and one of the largest museum-connected community art schools in the United States (museum website, about page).

The museum states that for 90 years or more it has acquired, protected and presented its collection; the Form 990 lists tax exemption from October 1942 (museum website; ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer).

What is there: more than 8,500 objects, with depth in European and American paintings and sculpture from the 15th century to the present and extensive decorative and applied arts, including ethnographic study collections dating back five millennia (museum website, about page).
funding_verdict: Flint Institute of Arts: donations, a county arts millage and the Mott Foundation, with earned income under a tenth

name: Kimbell Art Museum
overview: An art museum on a 9.5 acre site in Fort Worth, Texas, in a 1972 building by Louis I. Kahn, with a second building by Renzo Piano opened in 2013 for exhibitions, classrooms and a 298-seat auditorium (Google Arts & Culture partner page; Texas State Historical Association).

Kay Kimbell, who died in 1964, directed his foundation to build and run it; founding director Richard Fargo Brown joined in 1965 and the museum opened in October 1972 at a building cost of $6.5 million (Texas State Historical Association).

The collection is about 350 works from antiquity to the 20th century: European paintings, Egyptian and classical antiquities, and Asian, Precolumbian and African art; it grew from the Kimbells' 18th and 19th century British pictures and includes Duccio's The Raising of Lazarus, La Tour's The Cheat with the Ace of Clubs and Caravaggio's The Cardsharps, bought in 1987; it does not collect art made after the 1930s or North American art (Google Arts & Culture partner page; Texas State Historical Association).
funding_verdict: Kimbell Art Museum: paid for by its own foundation, built on the founder's bequest

name: Grand Rapids Art Museum
overview: The Grand Rapids Art Museum is at 101 Monroe Center Street NW in downtown Grand Rapids, a 125,000 square foot building with 20,000 square feet of galleries, certified LEED Gold in 2008, designed by Munkenbeck+Marshall Architects, appointed in 2002 (museum website, about page).

A constitution was adopted on 1 June 1910 establishing the Art Association of Grand Rapids, which became the museum; Della (Foote) Perkins was its founding president (museum website, about page). The museum marks 20 years in its downtown building in 2027 (museum website, home page).
What is there: the museum publishes collection highlights online and a Researching Your Art page; the pages read give no object count (museum website, collection page).
funding_verdict: Grand Rapids Art Museum: mainly contributions, with the Meijer Foundation funding free access

name: Hampton University Museum
overview: The Hampton University Museum is on the campus of Hampton University, Hampton, Virginia (Hampton University, 28 January 2026 release).
It was founded in 1868 and calls itself the nation's oldest African American museum (Hampton University, 28 January 2026 release).

What is there: more than 9,000 objects, including what the university calls the world's first collection of African American fine art; Jacob Lawrence, Romare Bearden and John Biggers are central to the permanent galleries, and the holdings are African and African American art (Hampton University, 28 January 2026 release).
funding_verdict: Hampton University Museum: university-owned, with foundation grants and donated art

name: Alley Theatre
overview: A resident professional theatre in downtown Houston, whose artistic director is Rob Melrose and managing director was Dean Gladden in 2022 (Houston Arts Journal, 20 July 2022).
The pages read did not state the founding year or the founder.
What is there: the Alley presents a season of plays and world premieres; Dear Alien was scheduled to premiere there on 8 May 2026 and run to 31 May 2026 (BroadwayWorld, 4 December 2025).
funding_verdict: Alley Theatre: mainly private gifts and one very large anonymous matching grant, with ticket income about a third

name: Mississippi Museum of Art
overview: The Mississippi Museum of Art is at 380 South Lamar Street, at the corner of Lamar and Court streets in downtown Jackson, with an Art Garden open in daylight (museum website, home page).
It began as the Mississippi Art Association in 1911 with a small group of paintings and became the Mississippi Museum of Art in 1978 (museum website, collection page).

What is there: more than 5,800 objects, strongest in 19th and 20th century American art, with Robert Henri, Georgia O'Keeffe, Andy Warhol and Radcliffe Bailey, and American Modernists including Arthur B. Davies, John Marin, George Bellows and Romare Bearden. Sara Virginia Jones left more than 300 prints from the 16th through 20th centuries, and Paul and Celia Mabry gave Modernist works (museum website, collection page).
funding_verdict: Mississippi Museum of Art: private giving, a growing share of state government money, and earned income

name: California African American Museum
overview: A state museum of African American history, art and culture in a 44,000-square-foot building in Exposition Park, a 152-acre tract in south Los Angeles owned by the state, with 15,000 square feet of gallery space (California state budget 2025-26).

Chartered by the State of California in September 1977, it began formal operations in 1981 in temporary quarters at the California Museum of Science and Industry, and its present building opened during the Olympic Games of July 1984 (California Assembly budget subcommittee, 7 April 2015).

The permanent collection holds 4,000 objects: paintings, photographs, film, sculpture, historical documents and artifacts, with an emphasis on California and the western United States (California state budget 2025-26).
funding_verdict: California African American Museum: public, paid by the State of California

name: REDCAT (Roy and Edna Disney/CalArts Theater)
overview: Downtown Los Angeles contemporary arts centre of CalArts (California Institute of the Arts) at 631 W 2nd Street, in the Walt Disney Concert Hall complex. It presents performances, exhibitions, screenings and literary events (REDCAT website).
Opened in November 2003 as an extension of CalArts into downtown Los Angeles (Wikipedia).
Named for Roy and Edna Disney: Patty and Roy E. Disney matched the Walt Disney Company's gift and named the venue after his parents (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: REDCAT: university-run, with foundation and arts-agency grants
